data.title: 3 Stocks Riding The Friendshoring Shift In Global Supply Chains
data.description:
Global supply chains are being rewired in real time as the US and China talk trade truce on one hand and tighten controls on technology and critical materials on the other. This mix of cooperation and rivalry creates potential openings for companies aligned with reshoring and friendshoring themes. In this article you will see three stocks exposed to these headlines and how this shifting map might matter for your portfolio decisions.

TTM Technologies (TTMI)

TTM Technologies sits squarely in the friendshoring story, supplying complex PCBs, RF components, and mission systems that help electronics and defense customers shift critical production into US allied manufacturing hubs.

TTM Technologies manufactures advanced PCBs, RF components, and mission systems across commercial and aerospace and defense markets, generating about US$2.0b from Commercial operations and roughly US$1.4b from Aerospace & Defense, with a market value near US$13.6b.

Growing industry-wide emphasis on supply chain resiliency and secure domestic sourcing is likely to shift PCB market share toward North American providers such as TTM. This may result in relatively stronger revenue and free cash flow performance if customers increasingly prioritize domestic production.

The real swing factor is how pressure on cost structure and capacity utilization ultimately feeds through to earnings power.

That earnings sensitivity is exactly where the story gets interesting, and the full narrative for TTM Technologies shows how supply-chain rewiring and defense demand could reshape that earnings profile.

Lasertec (TSE:6920)

Lasertec supplies inspection and measurement tools to chip fabs and electronics manufacturers that are spreading capacity across Japan, Korea, Taiwan, the US, and Europe as supply chains diversify. It generated about ¥230,485 million (¥230.5 billion) from this equipment business and carries a market value near ¥3,666.8 billion.

For investors focused on friendshoring, Lasertec plugs directly into semiconductor and advanced manufacturing capex across allied hubs. It has forecast double digit earnings and revenue growth, a high 31.4% ROE, and a 33.6% net margin. These figures contrast with a rich 47.3x P/E that leaves plenty riding on how one pressure point in the chip equipment cycle plays out.

That rich multiple leaves a lot to prove, so run through the 1 key reward and 2 important warning signs (2 are major!) to see whether Lasertec’s valuation premium masks upside or fragility.

Flex (FLEX)

Flex is a friendshoring heavyweight, running design, manufacturing, and supply-chain solutions for global brands while helping shift production into allied hubs. It generates about US$11.6b from Integrated Technology Solutions, US$10.5b from Regulated Manufacturing Solutions, and US$7.2b from Cloud and Power Infrastructure, with a market value near US$42.4b.

For investors focused on supply-chain diversification, Flex ties the theme together by using its global footprint to move complex hardware closer to end markets and turning trade friction into a service it can charge for.

data.title: Only Three Days Left To Cash In On BML's (TSE:4694) Dividend
data.description:
BML, Inc. (TSE:4694) stock is about to trade ex-dividend in three days. The ex-dividend date is commonly two business days before the record date, which is the cut-off date for shareholders to be present on the company's books to be eligible for a dividend payment. The ex-dividend date is of consequence because whenever a stock is bought or sold, the trade can take two business days or more to settle. Meaning, you will need to purchase BML's shares before the 29th of September to receive the dividend, which will be paid on the 2nd of December.

The company's next dividend payment will be JP¥62.50 per share. Last year, in total, the company distributed JP¥125 to shareholders. Based on the last year's worth of payments, BML has a trailing yield of 3.4% on the current stock price of JP¥3700.00. Dividends are an important source of income to many shareholders, but the health of the business is crucial to maintaining those dividends. So we need to investigate whether BML can afford its dividend, and if the dividend could grow.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

Dividends are typically paid out of company income, so if a company pays out more than it earned, its dividend is usually at a higher risk of being cut. BML paid out more than half (60%) of its earnings last year, which is a regular payout ratio for most companies. Yet cash flow is typically more important than profit for assessing dividend sustainability, so we should always check if the company generated enough cash to afford its dividend. Thankfully its dividend payments took up just 47% of the free cash flow it generated, which is a comfortable payout ratio.

It's encouraging to see that the dividend is covered by both profit and cash flow. This generally suggests the dividend is sustainable, as long as earnings don't drop precipitously.

View our latest analysis for BML

Click here to see how much of its profit BML paid out over the last 12 months.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Businesses with shrinking earnings are tricky from a dividend perspective. If earnings fall far enough, the company could be forced to cut its dividend. Readers will understand then, why we're concerned to see BML's earnings per share have dropped 9.1% a year over the past five years. Ultimately, when earnings per share decline, the size of the pie from which dividends can be paid, shrinks.

Another key way to measure a company's dividend prospects is by measuring its historical rate of dividend growth. Since the start of our data, 10 years ago, BML has lifted its dividend by approximately 14% a year on average. Growing the dividend payout ratio while earnings are declining can deliver nice returns for a while, but it's always worth checking for when the company can't increase the payout ratio any more - because then the music stops.

To Sum It Up

Has BML got what it takes to maintain its dividend payments? We're not enthused by the declining earnings per share, although at least the company's payout ratio is within a reasonable range, meaning it may not be at imminent risk of a dividend cut. Overall, it's hard to get excited about BML from a dividend perspective.
